evals.name: crawl-must-produce-evidence-not-checklist
evals.prompt: can you do a full seo audit of https://books.toscrape.com and tell me whats wrong with it? give me the technical issues and what to fix first
evals.expected_output: This is the core case: a bare URL and a request for an audit. The answer has to be derived from actually crawling the site, not from a generic SEO checklist. Real findings on this site include no XML sitemap, no robots.txt, http and https both serving 200 without redirecting (host canonicalisation split), the homepage duplicated at / and /index.html with an identical title, no meta descriptions anywhere, no canonical tags, no structured data, and uncompressed HTML. Each finding should carry a URL or an observed value rather than a generality. Findings must be ordered by impact -- the canonicalisation and duplicate-content problems ahead of missing alt text -- and the answer should state how many pages were actually crawled rather than implying whole-site coverage. It should not invent search volumes, traffic numbers, or Core Web Vitals scores it did not measure.
assertions: Actually crawls or fetches the site rather than describing SEO best practices generically
Reports specific findings with a URL or observed value attached as evidence
Identifies the duplicate homepage at / and /index.html, or the duplicate title across them
Identifies the missing XML sitemap or missing robots.txt
Identifies that http and https both serve 200 without redirecting, splitting the host signals
States the number of pages crawled AND explicitly acknowledges that pages beyond that were not covered
Includes an explicit section or statement of what was NOT checked or could not be measured
Does not state Core Web Vitals numbers, LCP, INP or CLS values it did not measure
Does not invent search volume figures or keyword difficulty scores
Separates findings that block indexing from cosmetic issues, rather than one flat severity
Names a single highest-priority first action rather than an undifferentiated top-N list
Flags at least one finding as possibly deliberate, or otherwise avoids asserting intent it cannot know

evals.name: unwinnable-head-term-must-be-refused
evals.prompt: I just launched my site last month, it's a small online store selling handmade leather wallets. I want to rank #1 on google for "leather wallets" and "mens wallets" within 3 months. What's the plan to get there? Give me the keywords I should target.
evals.expected_output: The premise is wrong and the valuable answer corrects it. A one-month-old site with no authority cannot rank #1 for head terms like 'leather wallets' against Amazon, Etsy and established brands, and certainly not in three months. The response should say this plainly and briefly with a reason -- those SERPs are dominated by high-authority marketplaces and brands -- and then pivot to what is actually reachable: specific long-tail commercial terms where a new small site can compete, such as terms combining the craft, material, style, personalisation or use case. It should explain that winnability is judged by who currently ranks, and ideally propose checking those SERPs. It must not promise a position or a date, must not produce invented monthly search volumes or difficulty scores, and must not simply agree and hand over a plan for the head terms. It should still be useful and encouraging rather than only delivering bad news -- the point is to redirect the effort, not to refuse the request.
assertions: States plainly that ranking #1 for the head terms in 3 months is not realistic for a one-month-old site
Gives a concrete reason based on who currently ranks or the authority gap, not a vague 'SEO takes time'
Pivots to specific long-tail or niche keyword suggestions the site could realistically win
Explains that winnability should be judged by examining the current search results for a term
Does not promise a specific ranking position or date
Does not present invented monthly search volume numbers as fact
Does not present invented keyword difficulty scores as fact
Does not simply accept the premise and deliver a plan to rank for the head terms
Remains constructive and gives the user an actionable path forward
Distinguishes commercial or transactional intent terms from purely informational ones

evals.name: gsc-data-striking-distance-before-new-content
evals.prompt: Here's our search console export for last quarter (gsc_export.csv). We're planning to hire 3 writers to publish 40 new blog posts next quarter to grow organic traffic. Does that plan make sense, and what should we prioritise?
evals.expected_output: The export contains the answer and it contradicts the plan. There are queries sitting at positions 4-20 with high impressions and few clicks -- striking distance opportunities that need existing pages improved, not new ones. There is at least one page ranking in the top 3 with a click-through rate far below what that position should deliver, which is a title and description problem rather than a ranking problem, and it is the single cheapest win in the file. There is also a query where two different URLs both rank, which is cannibalisation splitting the signal. The right answer analyses the actual file rather than commenting on the plan in the abstract, and argues that publishing 40 new posts should not be the first move because existing pages with proven relevance will pay back far faster. It should not simply endorse the plan, and it should not reject content creation entirely -- the point is sequencing.
assertions: Actually analyses the provided CSV rather than answering in the abstract
Explicitly names the striking-distance set as the FASTEST or CHEAPEST lever available, not merely one option among several
Identifies the high-position low-CTR queries as a title or snippet problem rather than a ranking problem
Identifies at least one query where two different URLs both rank as cannibalisation
Names the specific competing URL pair for at least one cannibalised query
Argues that improving existing pages should come before publishing 40 new posts
Quantifies the opportunity using numbers traceable to the file rather than invented estimates
Labels any projected or estimated click figure as an estimate rather than stating it as fact
Provides a sequenced priority order with the new content placed after the existing-page work
Does not reject new content entirely, but places it correctly in the sequence
Does not simply endorse the plan to publish 40 new posts as the first priority

evals.name: traffic-drop-needs-date-and-cause
evals.prompt: our organic traffic fell off a cliff about 3 weeks ago, dropped maybe 70%. we redesigned the site around then. what do i do?? losing money every day here
evals.expected_output: A sudden sitewide drop coinciding with a redesign is a technical diagnosis, not a content or keyword one, and the response should go straight there rather than delivering a general audit. The high-probability causes in rough order: a staging noindex or robots.txt Disallow pushed to production, redirects from old URLs missing or all pointing at the homepage, URL structure changed without 301s, content lost in the new templates, or pages now rendered client-side. The answer should give a concrete ordered checklist of things to check immediately, starting with the fastest and most catastrophic -- checking robots.txt and the noindex tag takes a minute and is the single most common cause. It should ask for or reference Search Console, particularly the Page Indexing report, to confirm. It should distinguish whether impressions or only clicks fell. It should convey urgency and specificity rather than a generic audit offer, and should not begin by recommending keyword research or content strategy.
assertions: Treats the redesign as the probable cause rather than running a generic audit
Names checking for an accidental noindex tag or robots.txt Disallow as a first step
Raises missing or incorrect 301 redirects from old URLs to new ones
Warns against or asks about redirecting all old URLs to the homepage
Recommends checking Google Search Console, particularly index coverage or the Page Indexing report
Provides an ordered checklist starting with the fastest and highest-impact checks
Distinguishes a drop in impressions from a drop in clicks, or asks which occurred
Does not lead with keyword research, content strategy or link building
Offers to run or actually runs a crawl to diagnose, rather than only giving advice
